native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: From 1985 onward, white (NLSY79 cohort 3, NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC) respondents' family net wealth exceeded that of black (cohort 1) and Hispanic (cohort 2) respondents in every wave, and both the ratio and the absolute dollar gap widened: median family net wealth was $3,500 white vs $1,600 black and $500 Hispanic in 1985 (ratios 2.19x and 7.00x; gaps $1,900 and $3,000), $12,972 vs $4,800 and $1,600 in 1990 (2.70x, 8.11x; $8,172, $11,372), and $42,600 vs $9,800 and $2,562.50 in 1996 (4.35x, 16.62x; $32,800, $40,038) - nominal dollars, unweighted complete case. Real (CPI-adjusted) medians grew for all three cohorts (x4.20 black, x3.52 Hispanic, x8.35 white), so the divergence is relative: white median family wealth grew about twice as fast. The widening holds in the balanced panel (W:B 2.38->4.69; W:H 12.67->17.75), after p99 winsorising (unchanged; source already top-coded near p99) and in constant 1996 dollars, so it is not an outlier or 1996-attrition artefact. It is largest at and below the median (1996 white:cohort ratios 4.35/16.62 at p50 vs 2.10/4.39 at p90; zero-or-negative net wealth in 1996: 20.8% black, 34.9% Hispanic, 10.9% white). Secondary composition evidence indicates by 1996 black respondents' observed assets (residential, vehicles, items over $500) nearly matched white levels while median net wealth remained 4.35x lower, implying debts and unobserved financial assets carry the residual gap, whereas the Hispanic gap also reflects much lower homeownership (23.5% vs 37.4%). Scope: this cohort-sequential, unweighted NLSY79 sample, family/spouse-unit wealth, no causal claim.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Read data/nls_raw.csv as strings; verified empty string is the only missing code, no sentinel values, all non-blank wealth values numeric-parseable; 2) coerced wealth, cohort and 12 asset-component columns to numeric; 3) coverage/value-range audit (blanks 20.4/26.7/44.5%; negatives and zeros retained as legitimate; top-coding detected); 4) HEADLINE: unweighted complete-case median family net wealth per wave per cohort with means, p25/p75/p90, share<=0 and 1000-rep bootstrap CIs; 5) white:black and white:hispanic median ratios (2000-rep bootstrap CIs) plus absolute dollar gaps; 6) quantile ratios (p50/p75/p90) to locate the gap in the distribution; 7) ROBUSTNESS 1: balanced panel observed in all three waves (n=5,739) - medians, ratios, gaps; 8) ROBUSTNESS 2: p99 winsorised medians/ratios; 9) SENSITIVITY: constant-1996-dollar medians via external CPI-U and nominal vs real 1985->1996 growth multiples; 10) SECONDARY: composition decomposition under the blank->0 assumption with ownership rates and owners-only means, plus zero-filled means relative to the white-cohort mean; 11) descriptive Sample-ID table (no exclusions) and attrition diagnostics; 12) independent re-computation of medians/ratios with the stdlib csv module as a cross-check. All tables printed with cohort labels and year in the columns.

sub_hypo.text: White respondents had higher median family net wealth than black and Hispanic respondents in 1985, 1990 and 1996, with widening median ratios and absolute dollar gaps.
sub_hypo.context: Cohort-sequential NLSY79 sample; white denotes cohort 3 (NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC), black cohort 1, and Hispanic cohort 2. Unweighted complete cases per wave; nominal family/spouse-unit wealth; zeros and negatives retained; no causal claim.
sub_hypo.relations: White/black/Hispanic medians were $3,500/$1,600/$500 in 1985, $12,972/$4,800/$1,600 in 1990, and $42,600/$9,800/$2,562.50 in 1996. White:black and white:Hispanic ratios increased from 2.19/7.00 to 2.70/8.11 to 4.35/16.62; corresponding dollar gaps increased from $1,900/$3,000 to $8,172/$11,372 to $32,800/$40,038.

sub_hypo.text: Real median family net wealth grew for all three cohorts between 1985 and 1996, but white median wealth grew about twice as fast.
sub_hypo.context: Unweighted NLSY79 complete cases per wave; family/spouse-unit wealth expressed in constant 1996 dollars using external CPI-U; descriptive, not causal.
sub_hypo.relations: CPI-adjusted median wealth increased by factors of 4.20 for black respondents, 3.52 for Hispanic respondents and 8.35 for white respondents, indicating relative divergence despite real growth for every cohort.

sub_hypo.text: Widening racial/ethnic median wealth disparities persist in the balanced panel, after p99 winsorising, and in constant 1996 dollars.
sub_hypo.context: Unweighted NLSY79 robustness analyses for 1985, 1990 and 1996; balanced panel includes 5,739 respondents observed in all three waves; source wealth is already top-coded near p99; no causal claim.
sub_hypo.relations: Balanced-panel white:black median ratios increased from 2.38 to 4.69 and white:Hispanic ratios from 12.67 to 17.75. P99 winsorising left medians and ratios unchanged, and CPI adjustment preserved widening, supporting that the divergence is not an outlier or 1996-attrition artefact.

sub_hypo.text: Racial/ethnic wealth disparities are largest at and below the median rather than at the upper end of the wealth distribution.
sub_hypo.context: Unweighted NLSY79 complete-case family/spouse-unit wealth in 1996; zero and negative wealth retained; descriptive comparisons.
sub_hypo.relations: White:black and white:Hispanic wealth ratios were 4.35 and 16.62 at p50, compared with 2.10 and 4.39 at p90. Zero-or-negative wealth shares were 20.8% for black respondents, 34.9% for Hispanic respondents and 10.9% for white respondents.

sub_hypo.text: By 1996, black respondents' observed residential, vehicle and over-$500 assets nearly matched white levels despite substantially lower median net wealth, implying a residual gap carried by debts and unobserved financial assets.
sub_hypo.context: Secondary descriptive NLSY79 family/spouse-unit asset-composition analysis in 1996; unweighted, with asset blanks treated as zero, ownership rates, owners-only means and zero-filled means relative to white-cohort means; no causal claim.
variables: Market value of residential property respondent/spouse own, 1996
Market Value of vehicles respondent/spouse own, 96

sub_hypo.relations: Black observed asset levels nearly matched white levels while white median net wealth was 4.35 times black median net wealth. Debts and unobserved financial assets are inferred as the residual explanation rather than directly measured components of this comparison.

sub_hypo.text: The Hispanic-white wealth gap also reflects substantially lower Hispanic homeownership.
sub_hypo.context: Secondary descriptive, unweighted NLSY79 family/spouse-unit composition analysis in 1996, with asset blanks treated as zero; no causal claim.
variables: Market value of residential property respondent/spouse own, 1996
sub_hypo.relations: Hispanic homeownership was 23.5%, compared with 37.4% for white respondents, accompanying lower Hispanic median family net wealth.
